title: Sanjaya tells the Gita
hook: a blind king is offered sight to watch the war his sons are fighting, and he says no.
carry: shravana: hearing holy words is devotion
tomorrow: why does Arjuna sit down before the battle?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Udyoga days ended by the Ganga: Karna, the great giver, promised Kunti four of her sons, so she will still have five. Your line: dana: give what you can, expecting nothing back.

The armies are drawn up on the field of Kurukshetra. In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and waits. Then the sage Vyasa comes to him with an offer. If you want to see the battle, he says, I'll give you sight. And the king says no. He doesn't want to see his own family killed. He only wants to hear about it. So Vyasa gives the gift to someone else: Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counselor. Today the Bhishma book opens, and the Bhagavad Gita, which we've read before, comes back inside the story that holds it.
screen: `THE ARMIES ON KURUKSHETRA` → `THE BLIND KING REFUSES SIGHT` → `SANJAYA WILL SEE FOR HIM`

segments.voice: Earlier on the path we read the Gita verse by verse, as a teaching on its own. For these six sessions, we put it back where it lives: in the middle of a war report. After Vyasa's visit, the book doesn't go straight to the first morning of battle. Instead, Sanjaya comes back to the palace with terrible news. Bhishma, the grandsire of the whole family, has fallen. Days of fighting have already passed. Dhritarashtra breaks down, and then asks Sanjaya to tell him everything, from the start. So when the Gita opens with the old king asking what his sons and Pandu's sons did on the field of dharma, he is asking about something already over, the way someone asks after a funeral: tell me how it happened. Every word Krishna says to Arjuna reaches us through Sanjaya, spoken to a grieving father who refused to look. It's a report in a dark room, to a listener who chose to hear rather than see. And that's how most Hindus have met the Gita too: by hearing. The Bhagavata Purana lists nine ways of bhakti, and the first is shravana, hearing holy words and stories. It's why families play the Gita at home, gather for a katha, and listen at the temple even when the Sanskrit goes past them.
screen: `THE GITA PUT BACK IN THE STORY` · `THE TELLING STARTS AFTER BHISHMA FALLS` · `THE GITA, TOLD BY SANJAYA` · then, large: `SHRAVANA: HEARING IS DEVOTION`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and be a listener for a moment, not a watcher. Find the nearest sound, then the farthest one you can hear. Then, if you pray, listen to one holy word, Om or a name of God, said softly, or one verse of the Gita read aloud. If you don't pray, let the last sound be enough.
Bhishma Parva. The Book of Bhishma, the book of the Mahabharata that holds the Bhagavad Gita inside it. This week carried us from the Udyoga embassy, through Karna's two refusals, to this dark room.
Your line: shravana: hearing holy words is devotion. The Gita you know, told in a dark room. Tomorrow: why does Arjuna sit down before the battle?
